Cnnarunn TYpr <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Each monster has a tag that identifies the type of <font></font>
creature it is. Certain spells, magic items, class fea- <font></font>
tures, and other effects in the game interact in spe- <font></font>
cial ways with creatures of a particular type. Lists <font></font>
of monsters organized by creature type appear in <font></font>
appendix B. <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
The game includes the following creature types, <font></font>
which have no rules of their own: <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Aberrations are utterly alien beings, such as abo- <font></font>
leths, beholders, flumphs, and mind flayers. <font></font>
Beasts are non-Humanoid natural creatures, like <font></font>
horses and wolves, as well as most giant animals. <font></font>
Celestials are magical creatures, such as angels and <font></font>
pegasi, with ties to the Upper Planes. <font></font>
Constructs are magically created creatures such as <font></font>
homunculi, modrons, and shield guardians. <font></font>
Dragons are scaly beings of ancient origin, such as <font></font>
red dragons and wyverns. <font></font>
Elementals are beings from the Elemental Planes, <font></font>
such as efreet and water elementals. <font></font>
Fey are creatures tied to the Feywild or the forces <font></font>
of nature, such as dryads, goblins, and pixies. <font></font>
Fiends are creatures tied to terrifying Lower <font></font>
Planes, such as balors and hell hounds. <font></font>
Giants are towering beings with humanlike shapes, <font></font>
like cyclopes, fire giants, and trolls. <font></font>
Humanoids are people defined by their roles and <font></font>
professions, such as mages, pirates, and warriors. <font></font>
They include members of varied species. <font></font>
Monstrosities are unnatural creatures with <font></font>
strange origins, such as mimics and owlbears. <font></font>
Oozes are gelatinous creatures, including black <font></font>
puddings and blobs of annihilation. <font></font>
Plants are sentient vegetation and fungal monsters, <font></font>
such as myconids, shambling mounds, and treants. <font></font>
Undead are spirits and the reanimated dead, such as <font></font>
ghosts, vampires, and zombies. <font></font>
<font></font>

The Player's Handbook describes the nine align- <font></font>

<font></font>
Hit. Any damage dealt or other effects that occur <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
as a result of an attack hitting a target are described <font></font>
after the "Hit:" notation. <font></font>
Miss. If an attack has an effect that occurs on a <font></font>
miss, that information follows the "Miss:" notation. <font></font>
Hit or Miss.lf an attack has an effect that occurs <font></font>
regardless of whether it hits or misses its target, <font></font>
that information follows the "Hit or Miss:" notation. <font></font>

If an effect forces a saving throw, the effect identi- <font></font>

save's DC, a description of which creatures make <font></font>
the save, and an explanation ofwhat happens on a <font></font>
failed or successful save. <font></font>
"Half damage only" on a successful save means <font></font>
the target takes half as much damage (round down) <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
as targets that fail the save, while also ignoring all <font></font>
other parts ofthe effect. <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Daulcn Nou.rroN <font></font>
A stat block usually provides both a number and <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>

example, an attack might deal 4 (ld4 * 2) damage on <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
a hit. You decide whether to use the number or the <font></font>
die expression in parentheses; don't use both. <font></font>
Murrrerracr <font></font>
Some creatures can make more than one attack <font></font>
when they take the Attack action. Such creatures <font></font>
have the Multiattack entry in the 'Actions" section <font></font>
oftheir stat block. This entry details the attacks a <font></font>
creature can make, as well as any additional abilities <font></font>
it can use, as part ofthe Attack action. <font></font>

SpBrrcasrrNc <font></font>
If a monster can cast any spells, its stat block lists <font></font>
the spells and provides the monster's spellcasting <font></font>
ability, spell save DC (if any spells require a saving <font></font>
throw), and spell attack bonus (if any spells require <font></font>
an attack roll). Unless noted otherwise, a spell of <font></font>
Ievel I or higher is always cast at its lowest possible <font></font>
level and can't be cast at a higher level. <font></font>
A monster's spell can have special rules or restric- <font></font>
tions. For example, a green slaad can cast the Invisi- <font></font>
bilify spell, but the spell has a "self only" restriction, <font></font>
which means the spell affects only the slaad. <font></font>
Spell Components. The Spellcasting trait notes <font></font>
whether the monster's spellcasting ignores the need <font></font>
for certain spell components. If any spell compo- <font></font>
nents are required, describe the monster's use of <font></font>
Verbal, Somatic, or Material components to signal <font></font>
to characters that it is casting a spell. A monster <font></font>
that requires Material components has them. <font></font>
Casting Times of 1+ Minutes.If a spell has a casting <font></font>
time of I minute or more yet is listed in a spellcast- <font></font>
ing action, the monster doesn't cast the spell in just <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
one action unless the action's description states <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
otherwise; the monster must take the Magic action <font></font>
on each of its turns and maintain Concentration to <font></font>
cast the spell, as described in the Player's Handbook. <font></font>

LEcnNoeRY AcrloNS <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
If the monster has Legendary Action options, those <font></font>
are listed in this section. A Legendary Action is an <font></font>
action that a monster can take immediately after <font></font>
another creature's turn. Only one of these actions <font></font>
can be taken at a time and only after another crea- <font></font>
ture's turn ends. The monster can't take a Legend- <font></font>
ary Action if it has the Incapacitated condition or is <font></font>
otherwise unable to take actions. <font></font>
The monster has a limited number of Legendary <font></font>
Action uses, and that number is specified in the <font></font>
stat block. The monster expends one use whenever <font></font>
it takes a Legendary Action, and it regains all ex- <font></font>
pended uses at the start of each of its turns. <font></font>
Lrurrno Usecn <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Some parts of a stat block have restrictions on the <font></font>
number of times they can be used. Here are the <font></font>
most common ways that usage is limited: <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
X/Day. This notation means the stat block part can <font></font>
be used a certain number of times (represented <font></font>
by X) and that a monster must finish a Long Rest <font></font>
to regain expended uses. For example, a Reaction <font></font>
that includes "l/Day" means the Reaction can be <font></font>
taken once and that the monster must finish a <font></font>
Long Rest to take it again. <font></font>
Recharge X-Y. This notation means a monster <font></font>
can use the stat block part once. At the start of <font></font>
each of the monster's turns, roll 1d6. If the roll is <font></font>
within the number range given in the notation <font></font>
(represented by X-Y), the monster regains the use <font></font>
of that part, which also recharges when the mon- <font></font>
ster finishes a Short or Long Rest. For example, <font></font>
"Recharge 5-6" in an action means a monster can <font></font>
take the action once. Then, at the start of each of <font></font>
the monster's turns, it regains the use of that ac- <font></font>
tion if it rolls a 5 or 6 on 1d6. <font></font>
Recharge after a Short or Long Rest. This nota- <font></font>
tion means the monster can use the stat block part <font></font>
once and must then finish a Short or Long Rest to <font></font>
use it again. <font></font>

<font></font>
<font></font>
Animal lords are the immortal spirits of legendary <font></font>
animals. They serve as the divine protectors of <font></font>
animals of their kind, and they appear as hybrids <font></font>
of humanoids and the animals they defend. They <font></font>
frequently change into giant, idealized versions of <font></font>
the animals they're associated with-albeit with <font></font>
glowing eyes. When contending with people, they <font></font>
sometimes appear as humanlike beings with subtle, <font></font>
animal-like features. No matter their appearance, <font></font>
animal lords exhibit the instincts and predilections <font></font>
of the animals they represent, tempered by their in- <font></font>
tellect and experience. <font></font>
Most animal lords make their homes in the Beast- <font></font>
Iands, but they occasionallyjourney to the Feywild <font></font>
or other idyllic realms. They rarely travel to the Ma- <font></font>
terial Plane, making exceptions only when a world <font></font>
faces environmental disaster or droves of animals <font></font>
are otherwise in jeopardy. <font></font>
Among the best-known animal lords are those <font></font>
that represent cats, hawks, lizards, and wolves, but <font></font>
animal lords exist for beasts of all types. Some an- <font></font>
imal lords even embody creatures that are rare or <font></font>
extinct on Material Plane worlds, like megafauna <font></font>
or dinosaurs. Using their divine might, animal lords <font></font>
can summon spectral animals, channel spiritual <font></font>
energy, and exhibit powers associated with one <font></font>
of three broad groups: foragers, hunters, or sages. <font></font>
These powers are tied to an animal lord's person- <font></font>
ality and traits associated with the creature it re- <font></font>
sembles. Roll on or choose results from the relevant <font></font>
Animal Lord Appearances table to inspire what <font></font>
creature an animal lord resembles. <font></font>

Legends claim the first behirs were magically cre- <font></font>

conflict between giants and dragons. The giants <font></font>
used their mastery of weather to alter the essence <font></font>
of blue dragons. The results were the first behirs, <font></font>
which served as hunters with a particular taste for <font></font>
dragon eggs. <font></font>
Behirs live in sprawling cave systems and elabo- <font></font>
rate ruins where they can make the most of their <font></font>
exceptional mobility. They are mindful of areas <font></font>
where dragons dwell, as most dragons view behirs <font></font>
as dangerous abominations and attack them on <font></font>

<font></font>
Beholders-also known as eye tyrants-number <font></font>
among the most notorious inhabitants of the Un- <font></font>
derdark. Few creatures in the multiverse are as <font></font>
loathed and feared as these maniacal horrors. <font></font>
A beholder's distinctive, globular body is domi- <font></font>
nated by an oversize maw and a gigantic central eye. <font></font>
Ten stalks ending in smaller eyes crown its form. <font></font>
From each of these eleven eyes, a beholder can un- <font></font>
leash a different magic power. The central eye can <font></font>
deactivate magic, while the smaller eyes emit rays <font></font>
that inflict various dooms-such as petrifying crea- <font></font>
tures, disintegrating them, slaying them outright, or <font></font>
other effects. <font></font>
Beholders possess utterly alien minds. Most ex- <font></font>
hibit paranoid, narcissistic, and megalomaniacal <font></font>
tendencies, and they act on agendas beyond human <font></font>
reasoning. While some keep to themselves, others <font></font>
force weaker creatures into their service. Still oth- <font></font>
ers cultivate grand ambitions, creating networks <font></font>
of minions to manipulate groups, settlements, and <font></font>
whole nations in the Underdark and sometimes the <font></font>
surface world. <font></font>
Few creatures loathe beholders more than other <font></font>
beholders. Every beholder views itself as the phys- <font></font>
ical and intellectual pinnacle of its species. To <font></font>
them, all other beholders are aberrant rivals to be <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
dominated or destroyed. Conflicts between behold- <font></font>
ers can last for decades and lay waste to vast subter- <font></font>
ranean realms. <font></font>
Beholders are a particular threat to adventurers <font></font>
because both gravitate toward mysterious ruins <font></font>
and sites of great magic. Many beholders collect the <font></font>
magic items and petrified bodies of heroes they've <font></font>
defeated, displaying them as trophies. <font></font>
BrHoronR LArRS <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Beholders lurk in cavern complexes they've carved <font></font>
using their eye rays deep in the Underdark or in <font></font>
lairs created for them by their servants. <font></font>
The region containing a beholder's lair is twisted <font></font>
by its presence, creating the following effects: <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Scopophobia. Creatures within 1 mile of the lair <font></font>
feel as if they're being watched. Any creature (ex- <font></font>
cluding the beholder and its allies) that finishes <font></font>
a Short Rest while within 1 mile of the lair must <font></font>
succeed on a DC 15 Wisdom saving throw or gain <font></font>
no benefit from that rest. <font></font>
Warping Terrain. Minor warps in reality occur <font></font>
near the lair; any creature (excluding the be- <font></font>
holder) within l mile of the lair that makes aD2O <font></font>
Test and rolls a t has the Prone condition. <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
If the beholder dies or moves its lair elsewhere, <font></font>
these effects end immediately. <font></font>

The blob of annihilation is a coagulation of cosmic <font></font>
entropy conjoined to the remains of dead gods. <font></font>
This malicious entity drifts through Wildspace and <font></font>
multiversal expanses inimical to life-vast regions <font></font>
where the chance of encountering it is low. <font></font>
The blob poses the greatest threat when disasters <font></font>
or nihilistic magic-users summon it to inhabited <font></font>
realms. Once unleashed, the blob of annihilation <font></font>
rolls across the land in vast, cosmic gyres, with <font></font>
fragments of the blob splitting off to engulf targets. <font></font>
The blob consumes anything it encounters, sweep- <font></font>
ing forests, villages, and fortresses into its mass. <font></font>
Within the blob is an expanse without air or gravity <font></font>
where entropic forces destroy whatever they en- <font></font>
gulf. Nothing can survive within for long. <font></font>
Only magic items and the corpses of gods and <font></font>
titans can endure inside the blob. Because ofthat <font></font>
fact, treasure hunters and theologians sometimes <font></font>
give themselves the deadly task of trying to retrieve <font></font>
something from within the blob. This quest usually <font></font>
ends in annihilation, but occasionally it results in <font></font>
the find of a lifetime. <font></font>
When the blob appears, roll on or choose a result <font></font>
from the Blob of Annihilation Contents table to in- <font></font>
spire what extraordinary thing remains within its <font></font>
goop. <font></font>

Arrogant and imperious, blue dragons are chro- <font></font>
matic dragons that crave control and collect follow- <font></font>
ers like other dragons hoard treasure. They seek to <font></font>
transform their territories into empires, domains to <font></font>
be feared by nations. <font></font>
Blue dragons have sharp features with piercing <font></font>
horns and scales that range from sapphire to the <font></font>
shades of stormy skies. They dwell in deserts and <font></font>
badlands, particularly regions with dramatic spires <font></font>
from whose tops they might see for miles. They <font></font>
seek lairs near sites of symbolic power, such as the <font></font>
abandoned fortresses ofgiants, the colossi offallen <font></font>
empires, or monuments raised by their followers. <font></font>
Regalia of rulership and artistic masterpieces fill <font></font>
blue dragons'hoards. These dragons have no inter- <font></font>
est in treasures that are common or flawed, prefer- <font></font>
ring one-of-a-kind gemstones, the crowns of fallen <font></font>
royals, and magic items capable of spreading the <font></font>
dragons' influence. <font></font>

Spiteful Storms. Dust devils and thunderstorms <font></font>

<font></font>

pallid skin stretched tight over frames that com- <font></font>

osyluths, these Fiends command weaker devils and <font></font>

fulfill their commitments to the Nine Hells. They <font></font>
slay those who renege on infernal deals, sending <font></font>
treacherous mortal souls to face unspeakable <font></font>
punishments. <font></font>
When not serving their diabolical masters, bone <font></font>
devils tempt self-obsessed mortals with promises <font></font>
of other creatures' adulation and obedience. These <font></font>
devils prop up petty tyrants, helping them grow in- <font></font>
creasingly calloused and amoral. <font></font>
Bone devils travel across the multiverse to fulfill <font></font>
diabolical orders. If left with no other choices, they <font></font>
might conscript mortals to aid them in their vicious <font></font>
goals. Roll on or choose a result from the Bone <font></font>

Ravenous corpse eaters, carrion crawlers gravitate <font></font>
toward places of slaughter and decay. In such char- <font></font>
nel environs, they feast on the dead with no qualms <font></font>
about their meals'origins or freshness. <font></font>
Carrion crawlers have segmented bodies like <font></font>
gigantic cutworms. From beneath their multipart <font></font>
maws protrude eight thin, lashing tentacles. Crea- <font></font>
tures struck by these tentacles risk being paralyzed <font></font>
and consumed. <font></font>
Carrion crawlers scour sewers, battlefields, ne- <font></font>
cropolises, and fetid wildernesses for corpses, cling- <font></font>
ing to ceilings to ambush smaller prey and to avoid <font></font>
competing hunters. They're drawn to light and the <font></font>
scent of blood, recognizing them as signs of food. <font></font>
These scavengers avoid ingesting inorganic ma- <font></font>
terial. Crypts with funeral armors sucked clean of <font></font>
their corpses and eerily pristine catacombs are signs <font></font>
of infestation by carrion crawlers. <font></font>

Clay golems are magical defenders made from earth <font></font>
and clay to protect places or communities. The <font></font>
materials used in creating clay golems originate <font></font>
from near the location the golems protect and often <font></font>
have special significance to their creators, such as <font></font>
clay from a holy site or bricks from a magical ruin. <font></font>
While some clay golems are masterfully sculpted <font></font>
to resemble living beings, others have only vaguely <font></font>
humanlike forms. <font></font>
These golems obey their creators' orders and pro- <font></font>
tect what their makers value most. Some still follow <font></font>
these orders long after their creators'deaths. Roll <font></font>
on or choose a result from the Clay Golem Orders <font></font>
table to inspire the commands a clay golem follows. <font></font>

Cloakers are mysterious Underdark predators, <font></font>
named by adventurers for their resemblance to <font></font>
hanging cloaks when they cling to walls. What <font></font>
cloakers call themselves is unknown, if they refer to <font></font>
themselves at all. Though they're undeniably intelli- <font></font>
gent, their behavior is often inscrutable. <font></font>
Cloakers sometimes gather in Underdark enclaves, <font></font>
but they rarely build settlements or form social <font></font>
structures. Most operate as solitary predators, lurk- <font></font>
ing in dismal subterranean reaches or abandoned <font></font>
dungeons-sometimes for months at a time-as they <font></font>
wait for prey to pass. They use their mottled hides <font></font>
to blend in with their surroundings. When unsus- <font></font>
pecting prey nears, cloakers unfurl and attempt <font></font>
to latch on and then smother their victims in their <font></font>
powerful wings. <font></font>
Cloakers delight in frightening foes. In addition <font></font>
to their methods of ambush, cloakers can create <font></font>
illusory duplicates of themselves and emit surreal <font></font>
moans that non-cloakers find terrifying in unex- <font></font>
plainable, primal ways. Cloakers might antagonize <font></font>
explorers lost in the Underdark for days, terrorizing <font></font>
and scattering them before attacking. They rarely <font></font>
converse with other beings, except to whisper eerie <font></font>
riddles to those they're about to consume. <font></font>

Cloud giants use the power of the skies to observe <font></font>
and subtly influence the world. These giants resem- <font></font>
ble humans with hair ranging from silver to blue <font></font>
and with skin in cloudlike shades from stark white <font></font>
to twilight hues. Curved canines grow in their up- <font></font>
per jaws, extending past their lower lips. In battle, <font></font>
they attack with weapons wreathed in storm clouds <font></font>
and throw roaring thunderheads. <font></font>
Most cloud giants inhabit citadels crowning tre- <font></font>
mendous mountains or magical palaces that drift <font></font>
amid the clouds. Many of these giants believe they <font></font>
possess similarly lofty status or purpose. Some view <font></font>
themselves as godlike beings who can manipulate <font></font>
and steal from terrestrial beings with impunity. <font></font>
Others claim their long lives and place among the <font></font>
clouds grant them unique perspectives, so they <font></font>
chronicle what they witness in the world below <font></font>
without interfering. In either case, cloud giants <font></font>
often possess fabulous magical treasures, either <font></font>
claimed from across the world or created by (and <font></font>
gigantically sized for) themselves. <font></font>

<font></font>
<font></font>

lie dormant in secluded wilderness, awakening only <font></font>
when disturbed or called on to serve once more. <font></font>

<font></font>
Culrrsr Acenoas <font></font>
'ld5 The Cultist Strives To ... <font></font>

<font></font>
<font></font>
age, or the world. <font></font>

Occurr Svunors <font></font>

Currrsr <font></font>

<font></font>
<font></font>
Currrsr FaN,q.rrc <font></font>

<font></font>
<font></font>
Currrsr HrrnopnlNr <font></font>

place. While the angel might be called on in times of <font></font>
need, it encourages mortal heroism. Should a deva's <font></font>
chosen champions carry out their charge, they ex- <font></font>
perience a revelation or the world is changed in line <font></font>
with divine purpose. Roll on or choose a result from <font></font>

A displacer beast resembles a gaunt, six{egged pan- <font></font>
ther with a barbed tentacle sprouting from each of <font></font>
its shoulders. This predator uses innate magic to <font></font>
displace light so it appears to be several feet away <font></font>
from its actual location. <font></font>
Displacer beasts hunt notjust to feed but because <font></font>
they enjoy killing. Once displacer beasts begin <font></font>
stalking prey, they can't be deterred until either <font></font>
they or their quarry is slain. While displacer beasts <font></font>
commonly inhabit dense forests, they might pursue <font></font>
travelers across great distances and even into cities <font></font>
or dungeons. More cunning than mere animals, <font></font>
these predators might set ambushes or lie hidden for <font></font>
days to bring down their prey. <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Displacer beasts sometimes pursue prey through <font></font>
portals to other planes of existence. As a result, <font></font>
these predators can be found across the multiverse, <font></font>
particularly on the worlds of the Material Plane, in <font></font>
the Shadowfell, and in the Feywild. These restless <font></font>
hunters can destroy a land's natural balance and <font></font>
drive other creatures to extinction. As a result, <font></font>
many druid circles and Fey view displacer beasts as <font></font>
deadly threats. <font></font>

Doppelgangers are supernatural beings with the <font></font>
ability to shape-shift into any humanlike form. <font></font>
Their mind-reading abilities aid them in creating <font></font>
near-perfect disguises and plucking secrets from <font></font>
unguarded minds. Occasionally, doppelgangers <font></font>
use their shape-shifting ability in more overt ways, <font></font>
transforming into unsettling forms to frighten foes. <font></font>

But after these disasters recede, the land is imbued <font></font>

ical fire and the half-remembered arcana of dead <font></font>
spellcasters. They rise from the remains of dead <font></font>
magic-users who were reanimated by sinister nec- <font></font>

for their creators or pursue ambitions left unful- <font></font>
filled in life. They lash out at foes with destructive <font></font>
spells and bursts of fire, wielding magic without the <font></font>
need for most components. <font></font>

Goblins obey those who accomplish the wildest <font></font>

making the loudest noises. Hobgoblins and forceful <font></font>

The deity Maglubiyet claims to be the god of <font></font>

Maglubiyet witnessed the destructive propensity of <font></font>

the Feywild to his realm on the Outer Planes. Since <font></font>

have flourished, with some finding their ways to <font></font>

Most gorgons are iron bulls wreathed in clouds of <font></font>
petrifying gas. Their metal plates vary in sheen and <font></font>
color, from sleek silver to pitted black. The oldest <font></font>
gorgons might be covered in rust, but this rarely <font></font>
impedes their abilities. These gorgons' stomping <font></font>
grounds are littered with the shattered remains of <font></font>
petrified foes. Many gorgons outlive their creators <font></font>
by centuries, misleading some to believe these cre- <font></font>
ations have natural origins and territories. Most <font></font>
such gorgons continue to follow age-old commands, <font></font>
guarding sites long fallen to ruin. <font></font>

bolical guardians called brazen gorgons. These gor- <font></font>
gons are hollow, bull-like automatons whose metal <font></font>
bodies glow with intense heat. When they charge <font></font>
their foes, the ribs of their frames open like cages to <font></font>
ensnare enemies and roast them within. Brazen gor- <font></font>
gons are often found in blasphemous sites dedicated <font></font>
to Moloch, other archdevils, or bloodthirsty gods. <font></font>

Hook horrors are beaked predators whose forelimbs <font></font>
end in massive, hooklike claws. They flourish in the <font></font>
cavernous mazes of the Underdark, with its miles- <font></font>
deep trenches and stalactite forests suspended over <font></font>
empty darkness, where they barrel through caves <font></font>
and swing across cavern ceilings. <font></font>
Hook horrors feed opportunistically on plants, <font></font>
fungi, and any creatures that come close enough to <font></font>
hook. To perceive their surroundings, hook horrors <font></font>
echolocate via a range of noises, from banging on <font></font>
rocks and their own bodies to vocalizations that <font></font>
sound like strange squawks, screams, or clicks. Only <font></font>
hook horrors know the meaning of these noises, <font></font>
but many people who explore the Underdark or live <font></font>
near deep-reaching caves have sought the sources <font></font>
of such sounds only to fall victim to hungry hook <font></font>
horrors. <font></font>

Known for their cowardice and toadying, imps <font></font>
serve devils and wicked magic-users. Their abilities <font></font>
to shape-shift and pass unseen make them skillful <font></font>
spies and adept at fleeing danger. Imps sent to sur- <font></font>
veil other creatures relate what they discover to <font></font>
their masters, but they frequently omit important <font></font>
details or cast events in the worst possible light to <font></font>
mislead their masters into following the imps' devil- <font></font>
ish council. <font></font>
Imps without masters delight in manipulating <font></font>
other creatures and inflating their own egos. They <font></font>
might take over bands of weaker monsters, or they <font></font>
might pose as helpful spirits and trick influential in- <font></font>
dividuals into pursuing nefarious ends. <font></font>

<font></font>

<font></font>
Habitat Coastal, Underdark; Treasure: Relics <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Kuo-toa have slimy, humanoid bodies and the heads <font></font>
ofgoggle-eyed deep-sea fish. They claim they once <font></font>
dominated whole worlds, their empires spanning <font></font>
land and sea under the blessings of piscine gods. <font></font>
The kuo-toa can't say what disaster brought their <font></font>
glorious civilization to an end, but elves, humans, <font></font>
mind flayers, and the kuo-toan gods bear the brunt <font></font>
of their blame. From the lands and seas of the sur- <font></font>
face, the kuo-toa retreated into cavernous trenches <font></font>
and Underdark seas. In these hidden realms, kuo- <font></font>
toa brood over all they've lost and forgotten, nurs- <font></font>
ing plots to avenge themselves for slights that might <font></font>
never have occurred. <font></font>
Kuo-toa hate the civilizations of the surface and <font></font>
the Underdark, believing themselves to be victims <font></font>
of age-old slights and ongoing conspiracies. Kuo-toa <font></font>
undertake contrived plots to propel themselves to <font></font>
dominance, often kidnapping people to learn their <font></font>
secrets or making dubious sacrifices to bizarre gods. <font></font>
To facilitate such plots, kuo-toa try to capture crea- <font></font>
tures alive using nets or strange weapons. Drow, <font></font>
dwarves, and gnomes dwelling in the Underdark, as <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
well as surface communities near submerged sub- <font></font>
terranean passages, are frequent targets for kuo-toa <font></font>

Kuo-toa frequently serve depraved masterminds <font></font>
such as aboleths and krakens. Such kuo-toa believe <font></font>
these powerful creatures are avatars of kuo-toan <font></font>
deities or gods in their own right. Kuo-toa might <font></font>
temporarily ally with other evil creatures, but these <font></font>

Kuo-roe <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Kuo-toa loot ruins and raid communities near their <font></font>
dwellings in the Underdark. Their shields are coated <font></font>
in sticky slime, which they use to disarm their foes, <font></font>
and they employ slimy nets to entrap victims. They <font></font>
usually strive to take their enemies alive and drag <font></font>
captives to their hidden lairs. <font></font>
Most kuo-toa follow the orders of their more pow- <font></font>
erful leaders out of a combination of faith and fear. <font></font>
In rare cases, a kuo-toa might abandon its commu- <font></font>
nity to live as a hermit or wanderer. Such kuo-toa <font></font>
might know much about the Underdark, but they <font></font>
live in fear ofthe strange gods they forsook. <font></font>

<font></font>
Some nefarious magic-users carry out forbidden <font></font>
necromantic rituals that sever their souls from <font></font>
their bodies to turn themselves into liches, masters <font></font>
of magic and undeath. With their souls preserved <font></font>
in hidden relics, liches puppet their own corpses as <font></font>
they pursue ambitions free from mortal bonds. <font></font>
Liches possess exceptional cunning and magical <font></font>
prowess, and they use their unnatural immortality <font></font>
to pursue arcane secrets few could grasp in a sin- <font></font>
gle life. Uncanny agendas lead them to plumb the <font></font>
secrets of life, the multiverse, godhood, and less <font></font>
fathomable topics. Careless of mortal lives or de- <font></font>
sires, liches go to any lengths to achieve their goals. <font></font>
A lich's age and origin influences its form. Older <font></font>
liches appear as little more than brittle skeletons <font></font>
clad in the rotten finery of forgotten empires, while <font></font>
younger liches more closely resemble living crea- <font></font>
tures and are clad in contemporary garb. Many <font></font>
cloak themselves in illusions of their idealized mor- <font></font>
tal forms. <font></font>
Although liches don't fear death, they're not free <font></font>
from the ravages of time. Over ages, some liches <font></font>
lose their connection to time and the physical <font></font>
world, degenerating into demiliches. <font></font>

The process of becoming a lich is involved, dan- <font></font>
gerous, and unique to each would-be lich. If the <font></font>
rite succeeds, the lich's soul is bound to a spirit jar, <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
a specially prepared magical repository. This relic <font></font>
anchors the lich's spirit to the world and preserves <font></font>
it should the lich's body be destroyed. A lich can <font></font>
be slain only if its spirit jar is ruined. As such, a <font></font>
lich goes to great lengths to hide and protect its <font></font>
spirit jar. <font></font>
Spirit jars are typically small, well-made objects <font></font>
that were meaningful to a lich in life. Roll on or <font></font>
choose a result from the Lich Spirit Jar table to in- <font></font>
spire where a lich hides its soul. <font></font>

<font></font>
Magmins divide all things into two categories: <font></font>
things that are on fire and things that should be on <font></font>
fire. With bodies of flame and magmatic rock, these <font></font>
halfling-size creatures delight in setting fires. They <font></font>
do so not out of malice but out of enthusiasm for <font></font>
primal fire. They don't consider that objects have <font></font>
value beyond kindling or that creatures can be <font></font>
harmed by flames. If such concepts are explained to <font></font>
them, they find the ideas difficult to grasp and don't <font></font>
remember them for long. Rather, they relish every <font></font>
opportunity to set flammable things alight, delight- <font></font>
ing in igniting paper, wooden structures, and explo- <font></font>
sives. Magmins are dangerous even in death, since <font></font>
they explode when they're destroyed, their flames <font></font>
igniting combustible materials nearby. <font></font>
Magmins might be conjured by magic-users to <font></font>
harry foes or might escape the Elemental Plane <font></font>
of Fire through portals or rifts that lead to other <font></font>
realms. They're attracted to places of intense heat, <font></font>
such as volcanoes and rivers of magma. If they <font></font>
can't find such favored conditions, magmins ea- <font></font>
gerly burn structures or start wildfires to entertain <font></font>
themselves. <font></font>

Mephits are mean-spirited tricksters that dwell on <font></font>
the Elemental Planes. The six most prominent types <font></font>
of mephits resemble halfling-size gargoyles with <font></font>
wings, exaggerated features, and bodies composed <font></font>
of two elements. Most live self-interested exis- <font></font>
tences, indulging their warped senses of humor or <font></font>
overblown egos on their home planes of existence. <font></font>
Some serve as messengers or spies for genies or <font></font>
magic-users. <font></font>
Mephits resent leaving the elemental extremes <font></font>
where they make their homes. If loosed on the <font></font>
Material Plane or other realms, they lash out with <font></font>
nasty pranks or by tormenting weaker creatures. <font></font>
When destroyed, mephits explode in a burst of ele- <font></font>
mental magic. <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Dusr Mnpnrr <font></font>
<font></font>

Dust mephits are composed of air and fine earth. <font></font>

Icr MnpnIt <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Ice mephits have bodies made of frigid air and <font></font>

dropping ice into peoples' clothes. <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Mrq.c\da MnPHrr <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
These mephits embody the merging of earth and <font></font>

but they loathe magmins and attack them on sight. <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>

<font></font>
<font></font>
Beings of magic and machinery, modrons embody <font></font>
absolute law. These inhabitants of the clockwork <font></font>
plane of Mechanus tend to the incredible mech- <font></font>
anisms of their orderly home and oppose chaotic <font></font>
forces across the multiverse. <font></font>
Modrons are parts of a vast hierarchy, spanning <font></font>
from quirky monodrones to the leader of their kind, <font></font>
the godlike Primus. Every modron carries out tasks <font></font>
assigned to it by higher-ranking modrons, doing so <font></font>
without question. Generally, modrons communicate <font></font>
only with other modrons of their own rank or the <font></font>
ranks immediately above and below them' Those <font></font>
more than one rank away tend to be either too ad- <font></font>
vanced or too simple for them to understand. <font></font>
Modrons excel at tasks that require patience and <font></font>
precision, but they have little understanding of non- <font></font>
literal concepts such as art or humor. They have no <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
egos; they have only their work and the certainty <font></font>
that multiversal law depends on their efficacy. <font></font>
In rare cases, a modron goes rogue and develops <font></font>
its own will. In these cases, other modrons are sent <font></font>
to recover or destroy their malfunctioning kin. <font></font>

Mysterious rites and mighty faith can tie spirits to <font></font>
their corpses, binding them to their remains for all <font></font>
time. Should their resting places be violated, these <font></font>
beings, known as mummies, reanimate their deteri- <font></font>
orating bodies to restore the sanctity of their tombs <font></font>
and punish those who disturbed their rest. <font></font>
Mummies pursue those who offend them, typ- <font></font>
ically mortals who desecrate their resting places, <font></font>
steal their burial treasures, or defile sites tied <font></font>
to their faith. With undying rage, these ancient <font></font>
corpses go to extreme lengths to avenge themselves <font></font>
and restore what they need to find peace. <font></font>
A mummy might look frail, but its body possesses <font></font>
supernatural strength, and its gaze can strike fear <font></font>
in the bravest hearts. Those who escape a mum- <font></font>
my's grasp might find themselves subject to a ter- <font></font>
rible curse. Victims of a mummy's curse gradually <font></font>
wither, their bodies rotting away until they're re- <font></font>
duced to dust. This curse can be healed only by the <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Remove Curse spell or similar magic. <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>

<font></font>

burial rites. Some are preserved through processes <font></font>
using linen wrappings or clay, but others are pre- <font></font>
served by peat bogs, ice, magic, or other means. <font></font>
Roll on or choose a result from the Mummy Res- <font></font>
urrections table to determine why a mummy has <font></font>
returned from the dead. <font></font>

Those desperate to escape death sometimes make <font></font>
terrible bargains with wicked deities. Devoting their <font></font>
hearts to evil forces, these villains gain power over <font></font>
death and a cursed immortality that binds their <font></font>
minds and spirits within a desiccated corpse. Freed <font></font>
from mortal concerns, these mummy lords pursue <font></font>
their obsessions across ages. <font></font>
Most mummy lords linger amid the ruins of an- <font></font>
cient palaces or temples where they once held sway. <font></font>
Their age-old faith and ties to deathly forces grant <font></font>
them fearful magic, which they use to sow ruin and <font></font>
animate undead servants. <font></font>
A mummy lord's heart embodies the pact that <font></font>
grants it immortality. Rather than bearing its heart <font></font>
within its corpse, a mummy lord removes and hides <font></font>
this accursed organ. As long as its heart isn't de- <font></font>
stroyed by fire, a mummy lord can return to unlife <font></font>
no matter what doom it meets. <font></font>
Mummy lords are usually consumed by ageless <font></font>
plots. Roll on or choose a result from the Mummy <font></font>
Lord Plots table to determine a mummy lord's an- <font></font>
cient agenda. <font></font>

Perytons tear out the hearts of those they slay, <font></font>

Piercers resemble stalactites, but each has a toothy <font></font>
maw and a single eye. They hang from cavern ceil- <font></font>
ings along routes frequented by denizens of the Un- <font></font>
derdark. Piercers might lurk for months at a time, <font></font>
waiting for any creature of their approximate size <font></font>
to pass underneath. When potential meals move <font></font>
below, piercers release their grip and plummet, in- <font></font>
tent on impaling prey in a single strike. If they're <font></font>
successful, piercers consume their meals and then <font></font>
slowly climb to a new ambush position. If they <font></font>
miss or fail to slay their targets, piercers attempt to <font></font>
squirm away, but they're easily dispatched by crea- <font></font>
tures aware of their presence. <font></font>
Piercers are the larval form of ropers. Young <font></font>
piercers seek to move as far from ropers as they can <font></font>
to avoid ropers'undiscerning hunger. Many piercers <font></font>
migrate vast distances through the Underdark, of- <font></font>
ten to caverns or buried ruins near the surface. <font></font>

The term "pirate" encompasses a broad range of <font></font>
seafarers, including vicious sea rovers, dogged pri- <font></font>
vateers, cursed treasure hunters, and others who <font></font>
seek riches and fame on the seas. <font></font>
Pirates might be allies, foes, wild cards, or some <font></font>
combination thereof. While they are the bane of <font></font>
merchants and coastal communities, they know <font></font>
secrets ofthe sea and how to avoid aquatic threats. <font></font>
More unusual pirates set their sights beyond <font></font>
the waves, using airships, spelljamming vessels, <font></font>
plane-shifting craft, or stranger vehicles to explore <font></font>
and raid incredible realms. <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Prnann <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Along with being competent warriors, pirates are <font></font>
accomplished seafarers who know how to sail and <font></font>
maintain a ship. While some loyally follow their <font></font>
captains' orders, others place greed, superstition, or <font></font>
self-preservation over duty. <font></font>
Prnerr CeprerN <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Pirate captains command crews of pirates, dictating <font></font>
their destinations and targets. Captains cultivate <font></font>
fearsome and theatrical reputations, painting them- <font></font>
selves as larger-than-life characters to terrorize <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
their foes, ensure the obedience of their crews, <font></font>
and attract followers to their banner. Many have <font></font>
colorful nicknames inspired by signature traits and <font></font>
deeds. <font></font>

SITIUANDERS <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Serpentine Artists of the Inferno <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Habitat Planar (Elemental Plane of Fire), Underdark; <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Treasure: Armaments <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
Salamanders are serpentine denizens of the El- <font></font>
emental Plane of Fire. They believe that flames <font></font>
expose the purest forms of all things and delight in <font></font>
burning and melting things, seeing fleeting beauty <font></font>
and striking nuances in blazes consuming different <font></font>
fuels-ancient forests, artistic masterpieces, or liv- <font></font>
ing creatures. To salamanders, those that can't en- <font></font>
dure their flames are nothing but ashes in disguise. <font></font>
They harbor malice toward few creatures, but they <font></font>
consider creating remarkable flames more import- <font></font>
ant than the pain and Ioss their fires cause. <font></font>
Salamanders are typically content to dwell on <font></font>
the Elemental Plane of Fire, creating strange, tem- <font></font>
porary art amid the flames. Some travel to other <font></font>
planes of existence and worlds to experience the <font></font>
flames of other realms or create conflagrations of <font></font>
unprecedented scale. <font></font>

Among the most devastating creatures in existence, <font></font>
the tarrasque is an engine of catastrophe and a <font></font>
ruiner of nations. A terror of massive size and over- <font></font>
whelming might, this primeval destroyer survives <font></font>
from the earliest epochs of the Material Plane, <font></font>
when it served as a weapon of immortal forces. <font></font>
Since then, the tarrasque has slumbered in secret, <font></font>
rising every few ages to usher in eras of destruction <font></font>
The tarrasque is a bipedal, prehistoric Monstros- <font></font>
ity that stands over seventy feet tall. Bristling with <font></font>
horns and spikes, its spiny carapace deflects harm <font></font>
and can reflect magical attacks. <font></font>
<font></font>
<font></font>
The tarrasque is a creature oftireless rage. It <font></font>
lashes out at any creature that catches its atten- <font></font>
tion, thrashing with claws and its mighty tail while <font></font>
swallowing smaller beings whole. It seems to take <font></font>
instinctual offense at the works of lesser beings, <font></font>
venting its rage at buildings, bridges, ships, and <font></font>
monuments. The larger a structure or foe is, the <font></font>
greater the tarrasque's wrath. <font></font>
It is a mystery what-if anything-calms the tar- <font></font>
rasque, but eventually it returns to its slumber, <font></font>
leaving the world irrevocably changed. While the <font></font>
tarrasque might be halted by incredible opposition, <font></font>
its threat can never be wiped from the multiverse. <font></font>
Whenever the tarrasque is defeated, another tar- <font></font>
rasque awakes somewhere else on the Material <font></font>
Plane. <font></font>

While the youngest vampires might be little more <font></font>
than bloodthirsty servants oftheir creators, the <font></font>
eldest possess incredible cunning and control over <font></font>
supernatural forces of the night. <font></font>
Undead vampires lie dormant during the day, re- <font></font>
treating to resting places hidden from foes and the <font></font>
sun's searing rays. Roll on or choose a result from <font></font>
the Vampire Resting Places table to inspire a vam- <font></font>
pire's grim sanctuary. <font></font>

<font></font>
Vampire familiars are living people who serve vam- <font></font>
pires, either willingly or due to coercion by their <font></font>
deathless masters. They channel deathly energy <font></font>
through their weapons, incapacitating unsuspecting <font></font>
targets and leaving their victims as helpless prey for <font></font>
their vampire masters. <font></font>
Many vampire familiars aspire to eventually be- <font></font>
come vampires, while others are magically charmed <font></font>
or serve as part of some terrible bargain. In each <font></font>
case, these vampire servants show signs of their <font></font>
vampiric corruption, such as corpseJike complex- <font></font>
ions, uncanny reflexes, and evidence of their mas- <font></font>
ters' repeated feedings. A vampire familiar loses <font></font>
its supernatural abilities and returns to its original <font></font>
Humanoid state if its vampire master is destroyed. <font></font>

they're opportunistic hunters that target unwit- <font></font>
ting livestock and groups of encamped travelers. <font></font>
Wyverns usually land only to finish off creatures <font></font>
they've weakened with their poison and strafing at- <font></font>
tacks. Creatures that fight back or take flight might <font></font>
deter wyverns, convincing them to search for eas- <font></font>
ier prey. <font></font>
Once wyverns overpower a quarry, they carry <font></font>
it to their cavernous lairs to either consume it in <font></font>
safety or trap it to eat later. Most wyverns don't <font></font>
hoard treasure, but their lairs are littered with the <font></font>
possessions of past victims. It isn't uncommon for <font></font>
wyverns to carry off chests, carts, or small boats <font></font>
along with their prey. <font></font>

ple orders, they rely on primal drives rather than <font></font>
thought. They fulfill commands by working tire- <font></font>
lessly or battering through foes, but they are easily <font></font>
stymied by barriers or unexpected circumstances. <font></font>
Zombies are usually created from Humanoid <font></font>
corpses, but the remains of other creatures can also <font></font>
become zombies. Such monstrous zombies might <font></font>
possess the strength they had in life or a measure <font></font>
of their supernatural abilities, but they employ such <font></font>
abilities haphazardly at best. <font></font>
